## REASONING

The question is a clean, single-factor controlled experiment: isolate the effect of soil clay content on the runoff vs. recharge partitioning of infiltrating water, holding forcing, vegetation, topography, and all other soil attributes fixed. This is squarely the "conceptual" archetype — no domain, no spatial sampling, no observations. The design is a synthetic soil-texture sweep at a single representative column, driven by one fixed forcing time series.

**Goal decomposition.** There is one primary mechanistic goal: quantify how clay fraction shifts the water balance between surface runoff (QOVER/QRUNOFF) and sub-surface drainage/recharge (QDRAI). Clay controls saturated hydraulic conductivity, matric potential, and porosity in ELM's pedotransfer relations — higher clay lowers Ksat, which promotes infiltration-excess and saturation-excess surface runoff and suppresses deep drainage. This is exactly a mechanism the single-column ELM can represent, because SOIL is one of the levers the runs can pull.

**Factor levels.** Clay from 5% to 55% — I choose 6 evenly spaced treatments (5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55%) to resolve the shape of the response curve (likely monotonic but possibly nonlinear near the low-Ksat end). Six is enough to see curvature without wasted runs. To truly hold "everything else fixed," each synthetic soil should hold sand/silt covarying in a controlled way (or hold silt fixed and trade sand↔clay) — this is a genuine open question because you cannot change clay in isolation; the complementary fractions must go somewhere. I flag this.

**Feasibility.** The partitioning target includes recharge/drainage, which is a slow sub-surface state. Per the execution limits, recharge and water-table states are initialization artifacts without spin-up — every column cold-starts at ~8.8 m water table and reads ~0 recharge while storage fills. So this design MUST include spin-up (or a WTD-informed warm start) for the QDRAI/recharge signal to be physical. With that included, the experiment is fully feasible. Surface runoff partitioning responds on fast timescales and is robust even with modest spin-up.

**Forcing.** One representative multi-year forcing period, identical across all six columns, so the only thing that differs is clay. A humid-to-subhumid period with a mix of intense and moderate storms best exercises both infiltration-excess and saturation-excess runoff generation.

**Validation** is optional for conceptual designs; here I validate against physical/literature expectation (monotonic decline in recharge fraction, rise in runoff fraction with clay), not co-located observations, since none exist.
